entities.name: human surrogate models of central sensitization

relationships.subject: capsaicin
relationships.evidence_quote: Capsaicin (8‐methyl‐N‐vanillyl‐6‐nonenamide) is an alkaloid found naturally in pepper (Nelson, 1919), which induces intense sensations of burn by its agonist effect on the transient receptor potential vanilloid‐1 (TRPV1) ion channel receptors

relationships.subject: capsaicin
relationships.evidence_quote: The use of capsaicin as a surrogate model inducing secondary hyperalgesia is very common, with more than 100 original studies reported so far.

relationships.subject: capsaicin
relationships.evidence_quote: Secondary hyperalgesia surrounding an intradermal capsaicin injection is the only model where central sensitization has been conclusively shown to be the underlying mechanism in translational studies in humans and animals

relationships.subject: gabapentin
relationships.evidence_quote: The hyperalgesic effects of topical capsaicin were attenuated by gabapentin 1200–1800 mg, versus placebo in 4 out of 5 studies

relationships.subject: opioids
relationships.evidence_quote: The opioids morphine, fentanyl and remifentanil decreased 2HA in one open and 3 placebo‐controlled studies

relationships.subject: ketamine
relationships.evidence_quote: One study found the N‐methyl‐D‐aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist ketamine to decrease heat/capsaicin‐induced 2HA, nociceptive reflexes and wind‐up responses versus placebo

relationships.subject: intrathecal adenosine
relationships.evidence_quote: Intrathecal adenosine reduced 2HA and DMA areas (Eisenach et al., 2002), but was ineffective by systemic route

relationships.subject: heat injury model
relationships.evidence_quote: This results in a first‐degree burn injury (redness without blistering) for less than one day, primary hyperalgesia on the site of exposure and 2HA/DMA in adjacent tissue.

key_findings: Of more than a dozen human surrogate models reviewed across 269 studies, five (intradermal or topical capsaicin, low- or high-frequency electrical stimulation, thermode heat injury) reliably induce secondary pinprick hyperalgesia and have been replicated across laboratories.

These models induce dynamic mechanical allodynia far less reliably, and their pharmacological profiles (sensitivity to gabapentinoids, opioids and NMDA antagonists but not to NSAIDs or most sodium channel blockers) can be used to screen candidate analgesics.
